papers.title: RegDesign-Bench: Benchmarking computational methods for cell-type-specific regulatory DNA design
papers.abstract: The de novo design of regulatory DNA sequences that drive cell-type-specific gene expression could enable precise gene control in synthetic biology, cell engineering and gene therapy. Various computational methods have been developed for this task, yet systematic comparisons that guide method selection for different design objectives remain limited. Here, we introduce RegDesign-Bench, a standardized framework for evaluating cell-type-specific cis-regulatory element design through a comprehensive set of computational analyses. Among the methods tested, strong predicted activity was not consistently accompanied by cell-type-selective accessibility or prominent cell-type-associated motif signals. Similarity to reference sequence distributions also did not ensure high predicted target-cell activity or specificity. These findings demonstrate that favourable performance on individual measurements does not necessarily extend across regulatory properties and library characteristics, revealing application-dependent strengths and limitations of current design methods. Overall, RegDesign-Bench offers a general-purpose computational framework for comparing and selecting methods to design regulatory DNA that drives cell-type-specific gene expression.

papers.title: SYNBRIDGE: A VERSATILE FRAMEWORK FOR BIDIRECTIONAL INTERCONVERSION BETWEEN BIOBRICKS AND GOLDEN GATE ASSEMBLY STANDARDS
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Component reusability and interoperability are fundamental to synthetic biology. While BioBricks laid the groundwork for part domestication, Golden Gate-based assembly standards, in particular Modular Cloning (MoClo), revolutionized multipart assembly. Despite widespread adoption, standardized conversion between these two popular frameworks remains challenging due to sequence incompatibilities. While de novo synthesis remains constrained by cost and sequence complexity, conventional PCR-based conversion suffers from off-target binding driven by sequence redundancy in multigene devices, unscalable primer optimization costs, and amplicon size constraints. To address interconversion from an engineering perspective, we present SynBridge: a closed-loop idempotent workflow for bidirectional BioBrick-MoClo conversion built around two core operations, Bri2Mo and Mo2Bri. As a proof of concept, we validated SynBridge by constructing a composite genetic system integrating a BioBrick module for LuxR-mediated RFP expression with a MoClo-assembled device for thermoregulated GFP expression. Quantitative cloning efficiency and functional characterization confirmed a robust and reproducible workflow that operates without requiring ad-hoc solutions. SynBridge provides a versatile engineering tool that ensures backward compatibility, maximizes part reusability, and establishes a standardized interchangeability framework suitable for automated procedures. papers.title: Synthetic Reconstruction and Characterization of Endogenous Bacteriophage Genomes from Desulfovibrio vulgaris .
papers.abstract: Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) caused by sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) is a major challenge in industrial infrastructure, yet the limited availability of well-characterized bacteriophages has hindered the development of phage-based strategies for controlling these organisms. Here, we present an integrated genome-guided workflow for the discovery, validation, and synthetic reconstruction of endogenous prophages from the model sulfate-reducing bacterium Desulfovibrio vulgaris Hildenborough. Bioinformatic analysis using PHASTEST identified seven prophage-like regions distributed throughout the bacterial chromosome, including five classified as intact prophages. Ultraviolet (UV)-mediated induction followed by whole-genome sequencing of purified phage DNA experimentally validated four inducible prophage loci (Regions 1, 5, 6 and 7) detected in all three biological replicates, together with a fifth locus (Region 2) detected less consistently, demonstrating strong agreement between computational prediction and biological activity. Comparative analysis further showed that prophage functionality was not always correlated with computational completeness, as one computationally "questionable" region exhibited robust induction whereas another "intact" region remained inactive under the conditions tested. Based on these results, one highly inducible prophage was selected for synthetic engineering. Three progressively truncated synthetic prophage genomes (approximately 36, 33, and 29 kb) were assembled using long-range PCR and scarless isothermal DNA assembly and verified by Nanopore sequencing, which confirmed accurate reconstruction without detectable rearrangements. Following electroporation into D. vulgaris and UV induction, the engineered genomes produced reproducible localized turbid phenotypes rather than classical lytic plaques, indicating that the synthetic constructs remained biologically active but did not undergo efficient lytic propagation under the experimental conditions examined. Quantitative PCR analysis of representative structural and lytic genes in wild-type cells revealed coordinated transcriptional activation by 21 h after UV induction, defining a practical harvest time for subsequent characterization. Collectively, this work establishes an integrated computational and synthetic biology framework for engineering endogenous prophages from anaerobic SRB. The approach provides a foundation for investigating temperate phage biology in D. vulgaris and represents an important step toward the future development of engineered phage platforms for MIC control.
papers.authors: Lim B, Fida T, Crippen K, Wilson R, Lee SW.

papers.title: Targeting phenol-soluble modulins: eco-friendly theragnostic strategies against Staphylococcus aureus biofilms.
papers.abstract: The growing resistance to antibiotics by Staphylococcus aureus and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a global health threat. Traditional antibiotics act on the viability of bacteria, whereas new ones are now increasingly targeting virulence factors. Phenol-soluble modulins (PSMs) are essential virulence factors that play important roles in inflammation, neutrophil lysis, cytotoxicity and biofilm formation. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar were used for literature search of articles published between 2010 and 2026. Green-synthesized metal nanoparticles (NPs) have been found to be capable of altering these mechanisms by inducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, membrane damage, and by interfering with the quorum-sensing mechanism of the bacteria, along with inhibiting the Agr system. Optimization of NP-based interventions can be supported by multi-omics approaches such as genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and metabolomics. Other potential methods of targeted PSM pathway and Agr pathway suppression are also available, such as CRISPR-Cas9 and dCas9, but there are delivery difficulties. The potential use of combining nanotechnology, gene editing, multi-omics, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology could allow for development of more advanced anti-virulence strategies against S. aureus infections targeted at PSM.
papers.authors: Chakraborty A, De A, Sharma S, Prakash Dwivedi S, Bhattacharya D, Lahiri D, Nag M, Singh Gill H, Pandit S.

papers.title: Efficient whole-cell bioconversion of indole-3-lactate by metabolic engineering of high-glucose-adaptive Lactiplantibacillus plantarum.
papers.abstract: Bio-production of the high-value health-promoting metabiotic indole-3-lactate (3-ILA) by lactic acid bacteria (LAB) and bifidobacteria remains constrained to micromolar levels. This limitation is largely due to pyruvate outcompeting indole-3-pyruvate (3-IPYA) for LDH and NADH, leading to lactate accumulation and suppressed 3-ILA synthesis. In this study, previously developed high-glucose-adaptive Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strains LP-D-4G and LP-D-10E were evaluated as chassis for enhanced 3-ILA production. Compared with the parental strain, the adaptive strains exhibited increased l-tryptophan (l-Trp) utilization and 3-ILA production during resting-cell bioconversion, together with altered pyruvate-derived product distributions and intracellular NAD(H) profiles. Systematic genome mining and heterologous expression in Escherichia coli identified five active lactate dehydrogenases (LDH2/3/5/6/7) and one aromatic-amino-acid aminotransferase (ArAT2). Co-expression of LDH7 and ArAT2 in strain LP-D-4G achieved 6.06 mM 3-ILA, 0.95 mol/mol l-Trp conversion, and a 3-ILA/(3-ILA + lactate) ratio of 0.31 mol/mol in whole-cell bioconversion. Furthermore, optimization of l-Trp and glucose feeding strategies improved 3-ILA production. In a scaled-up 150-mL fed-batch system, strain LP-D-4G overexpressing LDH7 and ArAT2 produced 20.09 mM 3-ILA at 96 h, representing the highest titer reported to date for LAB-based 3-ILA production. At peak, 3-ILA yield, productivity, and the 3-ILA/(3-ILA + lactate) ratio reached 0.84 mol/mol l-Trp, 69.45 mg/L/h, and 0.25 mol/mol, respectively. This study establishes a food-grade platform for bioactive 3-ILA production and demonstrates an effective strategy to reduce lactate and enhance 3-ILA by combining a high-glucose-adaptive chassis with pathway reinforcement.
papers.authors: Shi CR, Zhang XJ, Lu ZM, Geng Y, Chai LJ, Xu HY, Shi JS, Xu ZH.

papers.title: Production of recombinant human proteins in Komagataella phaffii using a sucrose-utilization-based selection marker without antibiotic resistance.
papers.abstract: Komagataella phaffii (K. phaffii) is one of the most widely used eukaryotic expression systems for recombinant protein production. However, its industrial application is constrained by reliance on traditional antibiotic-based selection and the inability to utilize sucrose. Based on the heterologous expression of the sucrose hydrolase SucF from Aspergillus flavus in K. phaffii, the strain acquired the ability to utilize sucrose. It was verified that this trait can serve as a dominant selection marker under sucrose-selective conditions, making SucF a selection marker for antibiotic-free strain construction. Under a selection pressure of 40 g/L sucrose, the gene integration efficiency reached 100 %, comparable to that of traditional antibiotic selection. Notably, this system enables the substitution of the original glycerol carbon source with sucrose for fermentation. To improve the selection efficiency of SucF, a triple mutant (T65A/R322Q/S323G) was identified through computer-aided protein engineering, exhibiting a 57 % increase in sucrose hydrolysis rate compared to the wild type. Structural analysis revealed that this mutation remodels the sucrose-binding pocket. Ultimately, the SucF mutant was used as a selection marker in combination with the histidine auxotrophic marker (HIS4) to achieve secretory expression of human lactoferrin (hLF) and human osteopontin (hOPN) in the GS115, and the resulting recombinant strain was free of antibiotic gene residues. This sucrose-based antibiotic-free platform in K. phaffii provides a promising strategy for green biomanufacturing and industrial production of recombinant proteins devoid of antibiotic resistance genes.
papers.authors: Han M, Li M, Jia R, Miao M, Zhang T.

papers.title: Programmable bacterial vaccine vectors: A Design-Build-Control framework for precision immune engineering.
papers.abstract: Live bacterial vectors combine intrinsic adjuvanticity, mucosal targeting, and programmable antigen delivery within a single engineerable chassis, yet their development has historically relied on empirical attenuation rather than systematic design. We present a Design-Build-Control framework, adapted from synthetic biology paradigms, that reframes bacterial vector engineering as a unified biotechnological problem. Design principles govern trade-offs among safety, immunogenicity, tissue tropism, and route of administration. Build-stage strategies translate these principles into genetically stable vector platforms through attenuation, balanced-lethal systems, and antibiotic-free plasmid maintenance. Control-stage tools, including inducible promoters, quorum-sensing circuits, and kill switches, enable dynamic regulation of vector behavior within the host. We apply this framework across major platform classes, including live attenuated Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, probiotic chassis, and non-replicating systems such as outer membrane vesicles, bacterial ghosts, and spores, and examine how biomaterial-based formulation, including encapsulation and mucoadhesive coatings, extends engineering control into manufacturing and delivery. We evaluate translational determinants, including genetic stability, environmental containment, and regulatory compliance, alongside applications spanning infectious disease, oncology, and veterinary medicine. We further assess the emerging role of artificial intelligence in bacterial-vector design, distinguishing established computational applications, experimentally validated approaches, and prospective uses that still require experimental validation. By integrating advances in synthetic biology, biomaterials, and computational design, this review presents programmable bacterial vectors as an emerging biotechnology platform and proposes a Design-Build-Control (DBC) framework for systematically evaluating biosafety, manufacturability, and clinical translation.
papers.authors: Bakhsh M, Kwon J, Haq IU, Riaz J, Kim CM, Lee JH.

papers.title: Taxus wallichiana zucc. (Himalayan yew): phytochemistry, therapeutic potential, biotechnology, and conservation perspectives.
papers.abstract: Taxus wallichiana Zucc. (Himalayan yew) is an endangered conifer of the Indian Himalayan Region and adjoining countries, recognised as a natural source of paclitaxel (Taxol ® ) and its precursor 10-deacetylbaccatin III (10-DAB). This review comprehensively synthesises current knowledge of its phytochemistry, pharmacological potential, biotechnology, and conservation, highlighting recent advances, research gaps, and future directions. Phytochemical investigations have identified diverse bioactive compounds, including taxoids (paclitaxel, cephalomannine, and wallitaxanes), flavonoids, lignans, and phenolic acids, contributing to its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and anticancer properties. Advances in tissue culture, metabolic engineering, and endophytic fungal research offer promising alternatives for taxoid production, potentially reducing destructive bark harvesting. Despite its medicinal and pharmaceutical significance, Taxus wallichiana faces serious threats from overexploitation, poor regeneration, habitat degradation, and grazing pressure. Conservation approaches include ex situ propagation, genetic diversity assessment, habitat restoration, and sustainable utilisation of renewable foliage and endophyte-derived metabolites. By integrating ethnomedicinal knowledge, phytochemical diversity, pharmacological applications, biotechnological innovations, and conservation priorities, this review provides a multidisciplinary perspective on the species' scientific and ecological importance. Future research should strengthen sustainable production systems, clarify therapeutic potential of its bioactive compounds, and integrate traditional ecological knowledge with modern biotechnology and conservation biology to support the long-term survival and sustainable utilisation of this valuable Himalayan medicinal conifer.
papers.authors: Reddy MC, Kumar S, Rajendra MP, Venkateshwar Reddy B, Ravula R, Anish K, Naveen Y.

papers.title: Biomanufacturing of Succinic Acid.
papers.abstract: Succinic acid (SA) is a key platform chemical with broad applications in biodegradable materials, pharmaceuticals, and food additives, and its market demand continues to expand rapidly. Conventional production processes for SA rely heavily on fossil resources, are associated with substantial carbon emissions, and impose significant environmental burdens, rendering them incompatible with global carbon neutrality goals and the ongoing transition toward sustainable, low-carbon development. Microbial biosynthesis, by contrast, utilizes renewable carbon feedstocks under mild operating conditions and exhibits high atom economy, offering a promising alternative to petrochemical routes. In this review, we systematically trace the historical development of bio-based SA, focusing on technological innovations aimed at cost reduction. We summarize the principal metabolic pathways involved in SA biosynthesis, and critically examine advances in native SA-producing rumen bacteria, metabolically engineered bacteria, and yeast chassis systems. Furthermore, we objectively analyze the application of non-food feedstocks in bio-based SA production and highlight that, despite the current lack of economic competitiveness, such feedstocks represent a crucial direction for the future green and sustainable development of bio-based SA. Finally, we analyze the commercialization trajectory and strategic landscape of bio-based SA both globally and in China. This review aims to provide a conceptual framework and theoretical insights to facilitate the transition of green SA biomanufacturing from laboratory research to large-scale industrial implementation.
papers.authors: Xi Y, Zhu X, Xu H, Tang J, Zhan T, Fan F, Zhang X.

papers.title: Carbon-loss-guided metabolic engineering improved carbon atom economy and industrial feedstock utilization for l-threonine fermentation.
papers.abstract: l-Threonine is a high-value amino acid widely used in the feed, food, and pharmaceutical industries, but its industrial production is limited by low yield. In this study, whole-genome sequencing of industrial strain Thr1 was performed, and the genome-scale metabolic model GSMM-iJHL1061 was reconstructed. The model identified 54 CO 2 -related reactions and predicted 0.89 mol CO 2 release per mol l-threonine synthesized, mainly from the PPP and TCA cycle. Attenuation of decarboxylation reactions involving ilvBN, lysA, gnd, and icd, combined with RuBisCO-Prk and cynT-pyc-based CO 2 fixation, increased the yield to 0.66 g/g. Deletion of 166 non-essential genes generated Thr9, increasing the yield to 0.67 g/g. Further introduction of maltose hydrolysis and sucrose utilization systems generated Thr10, which produced 132.5 g/L l-threonine in a 1000-L fermenter, with a yield of 0.68 g/g. Overall, l-threonine yield was substantially improved through systems metabolic engineering, providing a useful reference for constructing high-yield microbial cell factories.
papers.authors: Liu J, Sheng Q, Ye C, Dong X, Meng G, Zhao C, Wei A, Yang F, Liu J, Liu L.

papers.title: Engineering monocytes and macrophages for therapeutic control.
papers.abstract: Engineered monocytes and macrophages are emerging as therapeutic platforms for eliminating pathological targets, remodeling diseased tissues, and coordinating local immune responses. Early clinical studies support their feasibility, but target recognition alone does not ensure sustained function after tissue entry. Recent advances in myeloid-adapted receptors, context-responsive circuits, checkpoint and metabolic engineering, in vivo mRNA delivery, and stem-cell-derived platforms have expanded the strategies available to improve tissue tracking, control cellular plasticity, and sustain effector capacity. Previous reviews have commonly organized the field by disease, target, or platform. Here, we examine engineered monocyte and macrophage therapies as integrated pharmacological systems structured across four coupled layers-sensing, signal integration, actuation, and delivery-and discuss how their coordination determines tissue exposure, functional durability, and pharmacodynamic readouts across therapeutic settings.
papers.authors: Chen Y, Brown CE, Shi Y, Feng M.

papers.title: From oleaginous microalga to marine chassis: synthetic biology and process-aware biomanufacturing in Nannochloropsis.
papers.abstract: Nannochloropsis has developed from an oleaginous marine microalga valued mainly for eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA)-rich lipids into a credible candidate for marine photosynthetic biomanufacturing. Its toolkit now spans genome resources, efficient nuclear transformation, homologous recombination, CRISPR/Cas editing, marker recycling, defined integration sites, and modular multigene assembly. Researchers have used these capabilities to alter carbon allocation, triacylglycerol accumulation, EPA synthesis and lipid-class partitioning, carotenoid metabolism, recombinant-protein production, specialty-metabolite formation, and cultivation robustness. This review assesses whether these advances are sufficient to support Nannochloropsis as a predictable, reusable, and process-aware chassis. The evidence shows that the genus has moved beyond basic transformability. Targeted genome modification and pathway construction are feasible, and native and non-native products have reached biologically relevant and, in some cases, process-relevant levels. However, outcomes remain strongly influenced by genomic locus, strain background, intracellular compartment, physiological state, and cultivation regime. Platform maturation will therefore depend on reusable genomic architectures, reliable organelle-targeting rules, dynamic regulation, and phenotyping suited to iterative design-build-test-learn workflows. Strain design must also be coupled more closely to cultivation, harvesting, product recovery, and deployment. Product-specific chassis configurations are likely to be more practical than a universal strain for EPA-rich oils, pigments, recombinant products, and specialty metabolites. Nannochloropsis thus provides a useful test of how an industrially relevant, non-model photosynthetic eukaryote can become a more designable marine production host.
papers.authors: Wang H, Liu J.

papers.title: Insights into the structure-property relationships of biogel-based inks in 3D food printing: From hydrogels and oleogels to bigels.
papers.abstract: Three dimensional food printing (3DFP) enables the on-demand fabrication of edible constructs with customizable geometries, textures, and nutritional profiles. Biogel-based inks (BG ink ), including hydrogels, oleogels, and bigels, provide a highly versatile platform, as their rheological and physicochemical properties can be systematically tuned to meet specific processing and functional requirements. This review critically synthesizes recent advances in biogel-based 3DFP through a multiscale structure-property-function framework. It compares the roles of molecular crosslinking and water confinement in hydrogels, oil-structuring networks in oleogels, and phase organization and interfacial coupling in bigels, linking these structural mechanisms to ink properties and macroscopic functionality. Building upon these colloidal and interfacial architectures, the discussion then connects formulation-dependent properties with key printing parameters to explain the shape fidelity, structural stability, and sensory-related and functional properties of printed structures. These structure-function relationships are further discussed in the context of representative applications, including personalized and functional foods, clinical and therapeutic diets, artificial intelligence integration, and sustainable biomanufacturing. Current limitations and future research needs are also identified. Overall, this review clarifies the multiscale relationships among biogel microstructures, ink properties, and end-product performance, providing a scientific foundation for the rational design of next-generation BG ink and advanced 3DFP systems.
papers.authors: Zhang C, Zhang Y, McClements DJ, Xu X, Sun Q, Wang Q, Jafari SM, Dai L.
papers.journal: Advances in colloid and interface science

papers.title: Microalgae-based removal and biodegradation of antibiotics: mechanisms, synergistic consortia, and engineering prospects.
papers.abstract: Antibiotic pollution in aquatic environments drives the spread of resistance genes and threatens ecosystem health. Microalgae offer a dual-function platform that both senses antibiotic stress and actively removes these contaminants. This review synthesizes current knowledge on microalgae-based antibiotic removal and biotransformation, emphasizing the integration of biosorption, enzyme-mediated transformation-primarily via cytochrome P450 and nitroreductase-and co‑metabolic processes. We highlight the phycosphere as a dynamic interface where symbiotic bacteria enhance algal survival and pollutant removal, while also modulating the enrichment and dissemination of resistance genes. Algal-bacterial granular sludge systems illustrate the practical potential of this synergy, achieving efficient antibiotic removal and suppression of resistance propagation. Emerging tools such as immobilization, synthetic biology, and machine learning show potential to further improve system robustness and may facilitate precision process control, although their scalability and long-term performance remain to be validated. By linking fundamental mechanisms with engineering strategies, this review provides a framework for developing sustainable, low-carbon bioremediation technologies aligned with global antimicrobial resistance action plans.
papers.authors: Liu J, Zhang J, Jiang M, Lin X, Peng C.

papers.title: Microbial cell factories for gamma-linolenic acid biosynthesis: metabolic engineering, downstream processing, and future perspectives
papers.authors: Qiao J, Wang W, Duan P, Zhang Z, Yang R, Cui H, Li X.

papers.title: Microbial cell factories for gamma-linolenic acid biosynthesis: metabolic engineering, downstream processing, and future perspectives.
papers.abstract: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) is a vital anti-inflammatory polyunsaturated fatty acid, yet its traditional supply from plant seeds such as evening primrose and borage is constrained by low yields and climatic instability. Consequently, microbial cell factories present a sustainable and season-independent alternative for scalable GLA production. This review critically synthesizes recent biotechnological advancements in utilizing oleaginous microorganisms as production platforms. It systematically elucidates the microbial lipid biosynthesis pathways and evaluates strategies to enhance GLA accumulation, with particular emphasis on rational metabolic engineering. Furthermore, emerging technologies for microbial lipid production, alongside the latest progress in industrial-scale applications, are thoroughly examined. Finally, comprehensive insights are provided to guide the optimization of the entire value chain, ranging from upstream strain engineering to downstream processing.
papers.authors: Qiao J, Wang W, Duan P, Zhang Z, Yang R, Cui H, Li X.

papers.title: Modular reconstruction and multi-level regulation of Escherichia coli for efficient uridine production.
papers.abstract: Uridine is an important pyrimidine nucleoside with extensive applications in pharmaceuticals, food, and biomanufacturing. However, the microbial synthesis of uridine is still hindered by unsatisfactory titer, yield, and productivity. Here, modular reconstruction combined with multilevel metabolic engineering was employed to design and construct a high-yielding Escherichia coli platform strain for efficient uridine synthesis. Enhancing the pyrimidine biosynthetic capacity was initially achieved by introducing a pyrimidine operon derived from Bacillus subtilis and disrupting the uridine degradation pathway, thereby promoting de novo uridine formation. Further metabolic optimization focused on improving precursor availability and product accumulation by strengthening carbamoyl phosphate supply, increasing pyrimidine operon dosage, reducing uridine uptake, and optimizing precursor supply. To balance cellular growth and uridine synthesis, the Esa quorum sensing system was utilized for dynamic regulation of thrA expression, while overexpression of the 5'-nucleotidase YjjG substantially increased uridine production. Through the combination of these strategies, the engineered strain U20-2 achieved a uridine titer of 17.99 g/L in shake flask fermentation. An optimized two-stage temperature-controlled fed-batch fermentation process further increased uridine production to 105.68 g/L within 82 h, with a yield and productivity of 0.265 g/g and 1.28 g/L/h, respectively. This represents the highest titer reported to date for glucose-based uridine production in E. coli, and notably, the entire fermentation process was carried out without exogenous inducers or antibiotics. Overall, this study offers a highly promising and practical strategy for the efficient biomanufacturing of uridine and related pyrimidine nucleosides.
papers.authors: Sun Q, Huo Y, Chen Y, Tang M, Zhao Y, Sui L, Wen P, Yang T, Pan X, Rao Z.

papers.title: Orchestrating polyketide synthase-derived aldehyde metabolism for Streptomyces biomanufacturing.
papers.abstract: Advances in metabolic engineering have enabled the integration of diverse non-native reactions into microbial hosts, providing sustainable alternatives to petrochemical manufacturing. We previously developed a modular polyketide synthase (PKS)-based platform in Streptomyces albus for producing 17 diols, amino alcohols, and hydroxy acids. In this platform, terminal thioester reductases (TRs) release aldehyde intermediates that are subsequently converted by post-PKS enzymes to control product chemistry. Here we found that PKS-TR strains accumulated hundreds of genome-wide single-nucleotide variants, including missense mutations on conserved PKS and TR residues leading to impaired enzyme activity. Based on the hypothesis of aldehyde toxicity, we coupled TR catalysis with downstream alcohol dehydrogenases (ADHs) through gene co-integration or PKS-TR-ADH fusion to limit aldehyde accumulation. These strategies reduced genomic variability and increased diol production, reaching a total diol titer of 14.2 g/L in bioreactors, including 10.8 g/L 1,3-butanediol. Extending this approach, engineered strains incorporating PKS-TR co-integration with transaminases or the padA aldehyde dehydrogenase achieved 79% higher total amino alcohol titers and 145% higher 2-methyl-3-hydroxyhexanoic acid titer than previous reports, while eliminating diol byproducts from the optimized hydroxy acid pathway. These results establish TR-mediated aldehyde release as a programmable branch point and orchestrated downstream catalysis as a general strategy for improving the stability, productivity, and selectivity of PKS-based Streptomyces biomanufacturing.
papers.authors: Dan Q, Wang X, Chiu Y, Hwang S, Baerwald JJ, Li Y, Waldburger LM, Dou C, Rong Y, Tao XB, Li C, Qin N, Liu Z, Cheong S, Chen Y, Gin JW, Schmidt M, Sullivan RE, Backman TWH, Petzold CJ, Keasling JD.

papers.title: Plant-Microbe Interactions as Emerging Biomanufacturing Platforms for Iron Biofortification, with Rice as a Principal Model.
papers.abstract: Iron deficiency remains a major public health challenge in populations relying on staple foods with low iron bioavailability, including polished rice. This narrative review evaluates how beneficial plant-associated microorganisms may support iron (Fe) biofortification by influencing Fe mobilization in the rhizosphere, root acquisition, and subsequent transport to edible tissues. We organize the existing evidence along a soil-plant-grain-food continuum and distinguish measured outcomes from proposed mechanistic links. This evidence-based framework is described as a plant-microbe biomanufacturing platform in a strictly conceptual sense: neither plants nor microorganisms manufacture Fe; rather, their interactions can modify its mobilization and distribution. Most studies have demonstrated microbial effects on Fe availability and plant physiology, but fewer have established increased Fe in grain, and evidence for Fe being retained after polishing or absorbed by consumers remains scarce. Future work should integrate field validation, nitrogen and water management, Fe localization, food processing, and nutritional bioavailability. This approach may help prioritize testable interventions without equating microbial activity or higher total grain Fe with improved human iron status.
papers.authors: Ríos-Ruiz WF, Barrera-Lozano M, Torres-Chávez EE, Jave-Concepción HG, Torres-Bernal L, Pompa-Vásquez DF, Vásquez-Briones I.

papers.title: Smart carrier-engineered microbial consortia for precision nutrient delivery in next- generation biofertilizers.
papers.abstract: With the increasing demand for sustainable agricultural productivity under a changing climate, the advancement of new-generation biofertilizers specifically based on engineered microbial consortia and smart delivery systems has become an integral part of agricultural activities. The development of next-generation biofertilizers based on engineered microbial consortia and smart delivery systems has emerged as a promising approach for sustainable nutrient management. The drawback associated with conventional microbial inoculants is their inconsistent field performance, which is attributed to the limited viability of microbes under field conditions, environmental factors, and poorly controlled nutrient release. Recent advances in synthetic biology, microbial engineering, and biomaterials have enabled the development of beneficial microbial consortia for agricultural applications. Combining these engineered microbial consortia with advanced carrier technologies, including hydrogels derived from biopolymers, nanomaterials, bio-based polymers, and responsive encapsulation matrices, can enhance microbial protection, controlled delivery, and persistence in soil. The application of methods for encapsulating microorganisms, such as spray drying, ionic gelation, extrusion, and microfluidic encapsulation, can regulate microbial release and may improve microbial survival and rhizosphere colonization. Smart carrier systems are designed to protect microbial cells and regulate their release in response to environmental and plant-associated conditions, thereby supporting more controlled microbial activity and nutrient delivery. This review examines recent developments in engineered microbial consortia, advanced encapsulation techniques, and controlled-release systems for improving nutrient-use efficiency in next-generation biofertilizer formulations.
papers.authors: Chhetri S, Nagpal S.

papers.title: Systematic engineering of COPII machinery and cell wall remodeling enables gram-level secretion of recombinant human serum albumin with native-like structural features in Kluyveromyces marxianus.
papers.abstract: Recombinant human serum albumin (rHSA) is an important alternative to plasma-derived HSA, but its microbial production is constrained by the secretion burden associated with its large size and 17 intramolecular disulfide bonds. Here, we developed a systematic secretory-network engineering strategy in the food-safe yeast Kluyveromyces marxianus. The α-factor leader enabled efficient secretion and correct N-terminal processing of rHSA. A system-wide screen of 35 SEC genes implicated coat protein complex II (COPII)-mediated endoplasmic reticulum export as a major intracellular constraint. Combinatorial engineering identified SEC23/SEC13/SEC31 as the optimal COPII module, increasing rHSA secretion by 60.7% although with a reduction in growth. Screening of 13 cell wall-related genes revealed the cell wall as an engineerable interface. Combining COPII and cell wall engineering increased extracellular rHSA by 287.3% (COPII+gas1Δkre1Δ) and 316.0% (COPII+kre6Δyps1Δ) relative to TOP1-rHSA. RT-qPCR revealed strain-specific transcriptional changes in selected COPII-, ER folding-, and cell wall-related genes, while stress phenotyping, transmission electron microscopy, and cell wall staining supported strain-specific cell wall remodeling rather than overt cell wall damage. In 5 L fed-batch fermentation with defined nutrient supplementation, the engineered strains achieved high-cell-density growth and extracellular rHSA accumulation of 2.32-2.37 g/L. Far-UV circular dichroism, Native PAGE, and LC-HRMS/MS demonstrated native-like secondary structure, non-denaturing electrophoretic mobility comparable to serum-derived HSA, and all 17 expected intramolecular disulfide linkages consistent with native HSA. This work establishes a food-safe yeast chassis through multi-layer secretion engineering for the production of rHSA with native-like structural features and provides a generalizable strategy for secreting complex disulfide-rich proteins.
papers.authors: Lu X, Zhao L, Chen H, Wu X, Zhao W, Zhou J, Yu Y, Lu H.

papers.title: Advances in plant metabolic engineering through synthetic biology
papers.authors: Alsuwat H, Alvarez D, Al-Babili S.

papers.title: DNA Nanotechnology-Based Robotic Devices for Frontier Applications in Healthcare.
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, DNA nanotechnology has enabled the design of diverse programmable nanostructures, accelerating the emergence of DNA nanotechnology-based robotic devices (DNRDs) for advanced healthcare applications. Recent developments in DNA origami, DNA walkers, and molecular logic circuits have enabled dynamic and stimuli-responsive systems capable of functioning as logic-gated nanopills, precision biosensors, and autonomous therapeutic agents. These programmable devices also support cargo sorting, molecular actuation, and externally controlled operations triggered by optical, thermal, pH, enzymatic, or electromagnetic stimuli. Despite these advances, several challenges continue to limit clinical translation, including maintaining structural stability in complex physiological environments, achieving scalable and cost-effective manufacturing, and addressing regulatory and safety considerations, particularly those associated with immunogenicity, toxicity, off-target activity, unintended activation, biodistribution, and long-term biological fate. In this review, we comprehensively discuss the evolution, design principles, and mechanistic foundations of DNRDs, highlight recent technological advances, and critically evaluate their expanding roles in diagnostics, therapeutics, and synthetic biology. We further discuss current translational limitations and emerging strategies required to improve their safety, robustness, scalability, and clinical applicability. Finally, future directions toward the development of increasingly programmable, responsive, and clinically translatable DNRDs are presented.
papers.authors: Sarkar M, Yadav AK, Das A, Gandhi JK, Singh A, Kosara S, Singh N, Solanki R, Bhatia D.

papers.title: Engineering root development with high precision.
papers.abstract: Root development is controlled by dynamic interactions between gene regulation, hormonal signalling, developmental history and environmental inputs, creating multiple layers of control that can be harnessed for engineering. Recent advances in single-cell technologies, spatial transcriptomics and synthetic biology are beginning to resolve root development at the cellular level and enable increasingly precise manipulation of developmental programmes. Here, we discuss how lineage tracing, genetic recording of developmental history, cell-type-specific engineering and programmable genetic circuits can be integrated to understand and control root architecture. We highlight emerging strategies for engineering adaptive and context-dependent developmental behaviours, including history-dependent and reversible response programmes and rewired root-environment interactions. Together, these approaches establish a foundation for programmable and adaptive root system engineering in plants.
papers.authors: Bilas RD, Guiziou S.

papers.title: Evolution of ( S )-2-Aminobutanol Synthesis from Chemical Resolution to Biomanufacturing.
papers.abstract: As a pivotal chiral precursor for the synthesis of the antituberculosis drug ethambutol and antiepileptic drugs such as levetiracetam, Chiral ( S )-2-aminobutanol requires high optical purity for clinical safety. This review systematically summarizes the evolution and recent advances in its synthetic routes. Traditional chemical methods, including the 1-nitropropane and 1-butene epoxidation routes, suffer from severe safety hazards and heavily rely on downstream chiral resolution. However, both chemical crystallization and enzymatic kinetic resolution are constrained by a 50% theoretical yield ceiling and incur heavy environmental burdens. To break this bottleneck, in vitro multienzyme cascades utilizing amine dehydrogenases (AmDHs) and ω-transaminases (ω-TAs) have emerged, achieving 100% theoretical yield from prochiral precursors and >99% enantiomeric excess (ee) driven by a distinct dual-pocket active site model. Furthermore, synthetic biology has enabled de novo biosynthesis via whole-cell cell factories. It should be noted that the recently reported 45.3 g·L -1 titer refers to the upstream amino acid precursor L-2-aminobutyric acid (L-2-ABA), not to the final ( S )-2-aminobutanol product. To overcome bottlenecks like the intracellular toxicity of the intermediate 2-ketobutyrate (2-OBA), strategies including efflux pump engineering (e.g., rhtA ) and quorum sensing-based dynamic regulation have successfully boosted the fermentation titer to 45.3 g·L -1 . Finally, the industrialization potential of these generations of technologies is evaluated, highlighting that the transition toward in vitro continuous-flow microreactors and a hybrid whole-cell + cell-free architecture , combined with the integration of AI into whole-cell factories, represents a future trend for green and low-carbon manufacturing.
papers.authors: Wang BB, Chen CD, Han YJ, Tong WS, Gao HS, Ma W, Liu JY, Xu JZ.

papers.title: Evolutionary Diversification and Functional Roles of MYB Transcription Factors in Algae: Insights from Genomic Distribution and Regulatory Networks.
papers.abstract: MYB transcription factors (TFs) represent a conserved family of DNA-binding regulators involved in diverse cellular and physiological processes. MYB TFs are well-characterized in terrestrial plants, but their evolutionary history and functional diversity in algae remain poorly understood. This review summarizes current knowledge of the structural classification, evolutionary characteristics, and regulatory functions of algal MYB TFs. Bibliometric analysis of Web of Science Core Collection publications (1 January 2003-27 April 2026) reveals a marked expansion in algal MYB research since 2019, with emphasis on transcriptional regulation, lipid metabolism, and stress adaptation. Phylogenetic analyses indicate that algal MYBs exhibit lineage-specific diversification, despite retention of MYB domains conserved with land plants. Functional studies further demonstrate that MYB TFs regulate cell cycle progression, carbon-concentrating mechanisms, lipid biosynthesis, nutrient metabolism, and abiotic stress responses. Nevertheless, most algal MYB genes remain functionally uncharacterized. Integrating multi-omics with genome editing will improve understanding of MYB-mediated regulatory networks and facilitate future applications in algal biotechnology and metabolic engineering.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Luo C, Li X, Liang Y, Xu P, Xue A, Du H, Chen J.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Models to AI Synergy: A Roadmap for Predictive and Personalized Biology.
papers.abstract: Two paradigms now drive the life sciences. One is the explanatory depth of mathematical modeling, the other the predictive power of artificial intelligence. For decades, mechanistic models have offered a rigorous, hypothesis-driven framework for dissecting biological processes, while AI has proven itself at finding patterns in the large, high-dimensional datasets of modern biology. Each has delivered major advances on its own. Together they promise a synthesis that could redefine the boundaries of biological inquiry. In this review we propose a three-part taxonomy of integration strategies, namely AI-accelerated mechanistic modeling, mechanism-informed AI, and hybrid models spanning one-directional sequential coupling and bidirectional iterative systems, and we survey their applications in systems and synthetic biology, pharmacology and drug discovery, epidemiology, and neuroscience. We then examine seven challenges that stand in the way: interpretability, data sparsity, causality, identifiability, computational scale, multimodal integration, and validation and generalization, and we close with a view of biological digital twins, causal discovery engines, and automated science. Our argument is that combining these approaches is the principal task for a new generation of interdisciplinary scientists who aim to build a predictive and mechanistic science of life.
papers.authors: Huang L, Sun H, Huang Y, Gu Q, Zhang H, He D, Zhang W, Chen S, Xu D, Zhao J.

papers.title: Intratumoral microbiota in cancer immunotherapy: metabolic-epigenetic crosstalk and engineered bacterial therapeutics.
papers.abstract: The intratumoral microbiome critically influences immunotherapy efficacy by modulating the host immune microenvironment and epigenetic landscape through its metabolites. Microbial derived metabolites such as short chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, trimethylamine N oxide, and tryptophan derivatives reprogram host cell epigenetics via DNA methylation, histone modifications, and non-coding RNAs, thereby shaping anti-tumor immunity and driving either immune activation or resistance. In turn, the hypoxic, acidic, and nutrient deprived tumor microenvironment reshapes microbial composition and metabolism, forming a vicious cycle that further affects therapeutic outcomes. Given these pivotal roles, targeting the intratumoral microbiota has emerged as a promising strategy. Advances in synthetic biology have enabled the development of engineered bacteria as programmable living therapeutics. These engineered strains achieve tumor specific colonization, controlled drug release, and multimodal functions such as cytokine secretion, immune checkpoint blockade, STING pathway activation, and metabolic reprogramming. By enhancing immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy and synergizing with cell therapies, engineered bacterial therapy represents a highly promising approach to improve immunotherapy efficiency. Despite challenges in clinical translation including heterogeneity, anti-vector immunity, and manufacturing complexity, this strategy offers a new paradigm for precision cancer treatment.
papers.authors: Zhao N, Zhang H, Pang Y, Zhu L, Liu Q, Zhang Z, Shen L, He Y, Lin S.

papers.title: Mixed-Carbon Fermentation with Hydrocarbons and Fatty Acids for Enhanced Medium-Chain-Length Polyhydroxyalkanoate Production.
papers.abstract: Mixed-carbon streams containing fatty acids and hydrocarbons are relevant to polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) biomanufacturing, particularly for valorizing waste and upcycling plastics that yield chemically diverse substrates. This study evaluated fatty acids (C6-C18), hydrocarbons (C6-C18), and their mixtures for medium-chain-length polyhydroxyalkanoate (mcl-PHA) production by Pseudomonas putida (PP), Pseudomonas resinovorans (PR), and a PP-PR co-culture. Among individual fatty acids, decanoic acid (C10) resulted in the highest cell concentration (2.05g/L). Medium-chain-rich fatty-acid mixtures (C6-C12, with or without C14) promoted PHA accumulation, whereas C8-containing hydrocarbon feeds favored growth. The PP-PR co-culture grown on the mixed hydrocarbon-fatty-acid formulation HCFA-1 achieved the highest PHA content among the tested configurations (60.96wt%), with a titer of 2.11g/L. The polymers consisted predominantly of (R)-3-hydroxyoctanoic acid (HO) and (R)-3-hydroxydecanoic acid (HD), with (R)-3-hydroxydodecanoic acid (HDD) as a secondary component and variable amounts of (R)-3-hydroxyhexanoic acid (HHx) and (R)-3-hydroxytetradecanoic acid (HTD). C8-rich substrate mixtures favored HO, whereas C10-rich mixtures increased the HD fraction. Thus, feed composition can tailor polymer composition in addition to supporting microbial growth and PHA accumulation. Because HO and HD differ in side-chain length, these compositional shifts may affect chain packing and crystallization. Adjusting the HO:HD ratio could therefore help tailor flexibility and thermal behavior for packaging films, coatings, and other value-added bioplastics. Although PHA titers were modest, this study examined substrate-composition effects rather than high-titer process optimization. These findings link mixed-carbon utilization to tunable mcl-PHA composition and provide guidance for designing feed formulations for targeted bioplastic applications.
papers.authors: Bandara K, Mohandessi M, Bai X, Du X, Wan C.

papers.title: PRK introns provide modular tools for enhanced transgene expression in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
papers.abstract: Summary Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is an attractive chassis for photosynthetic biotechnology, but reliable nuclear transgene expression remains a major limitation, despite continuing advances in genetic engineering. One effective strategy is the introduction of introns into transgene sequences to trigger Intron-Mediated Enhancement (IME). Genomic sequences retaining endogenous introns often show higher expression than their intronless counterparts, as we previously observed for the phosphoribulokinase (PRK) gene. Here, we investigated the IME activity of PRK introns, using the first intron of RBCS2 (RBCS2i1), the current reference IME element in Chlamydomonas, as a benchmark. The first two PRK introns, PRKi1 and PRKi2, emerged as the most active candidates. We assessed their IME activity using two reporter systems, two genetic backgrounds, and multiple promoter–terminator combinations, and observed enhancements up to 35-fold relative to their intronless counterparts. Finally, we validated their performance using patchoulol synthase, a challenging transgene whose expression requires introns and enables the production of the high-value sesquiterpene patchoulol. PRKi1 enabled detectable patchoulol production under conditions in which a single RBCS2i1 intron was insufficient. Overall, our results establish PRKi1 and PRKi2 as versatile, MoClo-compatible IME tools and provide a modular, Biofoundry-compatible framework for optimizing transgene expression for synthetic biology and biotechnological applications in C. reinhardtii .

papers.title: Protein Self-Assembly as a Design Principle for Enzyme Immobilisation in Biocatalysis.
papers.abstract: Enzyme immobilisation is essential for translating biocatalytic processes from the laboratory to industrial applications by improving enzyme stability, recovery, and reuse. It underpins sustainable processes in pharmaceuticals, biofuels, and food production, but conventional immobilisation strategies involve inherent trade-offs. Covalent attachment prevents enzyme leaching but may distort the active site, whereas physical adsorption better preserves enzyme conformation but allows enzyme leaching. Furthermore, carrier-based methods frequently encounter mass-transfer limitations and may require external cross-linkers, hindering broader industrial application. Recent advances in synthetic biology and materials science have accelerated the development of protein-based materials for biocatalysis. This review examines protein self-assembly as a unifying design principle for enzyme immobilisation, enabling programmable assembly under relatively mild conditions to overcome key limitations of conventional strategies. We discuss naturally derived structures such as bacterial microcompartments and engineered systems including virus-like particles, elastin-like polypeptides, and SpyTag/SpyCatcher, which support programmable enzyme organisation and enable compartmentalised multi-enzyme cascade reactions. Building on this, a major focus is placed on catalytically active inclusion bodies (CatIBs). As robust, intrinsically self-immobilised protein aggregates, CatIBs represent a simplified, carrier-free platform offering potential process and cost advantages for industrial biocatalysis.
papers.authors: Vijayakumar S, Sunna A.

papers.title: Selective Recognition, Covalent Linkage and Chemical Exchange of Artificial Cells through Engineered α-Hemolysin
papers.abstract: Bottom-up synthetic biology aims not only to build individual artificial cells but also to connect them into higher-order systems that communicate with each other. Reported artificial cells communicate through partner recognition, physical connection, and chemical signaling that are typically implemented by separate molecular species. Here, we engineer the pore-forming protein α-hemolysin (AH) with the SpyTag–SpyCatcher (ST-SC) pair to integrate partner recognition, covalent linkage between cells, and nanopore-mediated connection of their lumens into a single protein system. Fusion of ST or SC to AH preserved heptamer assembly and pore formation, and allowed the two heptamers (AH-ST and AH-SC) to be covalently joined. Cryo-electron microscopy resolved the resulting head-to-head 14-mer assembly at 2.20 Å. Calcein leakage and single-channel recordings confirmed that the engineered pores remain functional. Mixing ST- and SC-displaying giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) resulted in partner-specific association between the two vesicle populations. Finally, photo-triggered release of a newly synthesized caged ethidium bromide (EtBr) in sender GUVs produced EtBr accumulation in receiver GUVs that required direct physical linkage between the two GUVs. This platform provides a modular route toward artificial-cell assemblies in which both connectivity and cargo exchange are programmable.

papers.title: Synthetic biology-guided modular engineering of the secreted cutinase Fo Cut5a with a carbohydrate-binding module improves poly(ester-urethane) depolymerization in Yarrowia lipolytica
papers.abstract: Summary Poly(ester-urethane) bioconversion requires efficient polymer-degrading enzymes and microbial hosts capable of processing the resulting monomers. However, the optimal modular design of secreted cutinases for depolymerizing insoluble polyester-polyurethanes remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a combinatorial synthetic biology strategy in Yarrowia lipolytica based on the fungal cutinase FoCut5a from Fusarium oxysporum . A library of 96 Golden Gate-assembled constructs, combining four secretion signals, four interdomain linkers, and six substrate-binding domains, was integrated site-specifically into the genome and screened for depolymerization of the polyester-polyurethane dispersion Impranil DLN-SD. The best-performing variant fused Fo Cut5a to the carbohydrate-binding module Tr CBM1. LC-MS analysis demonstrated release of adipic acid, 1,6-hexanediol, and neopentyl glycol, confirming ester-bond hydrolysis within the polyester domains of the polymer and additionally detected 6-hydroxycaproate, indicating oxidation of polyurethane-derived 1,6-hexanediol by Y. lipolytica . Purified Fo Cut5a- Tr CBM1 displayed unchanged activity on p -nitrophenyl butyrate but reduced Impranil turbidity 5.6-fold faster and increased release of 1,6-hexanediol and adipic acid by 76-fold and 220-fold, respectively, compared to the unfused enzyme. These results highlight modular enzyme engineering as an effective strategy to enhance polyester-polyurethane deconstruction and support Y. lipolytica as a platform for polymer bioconversion and upcycling.
papers.authors: Messina E, Papi M, Barile S, De Rosa R, Scarcia P, Biundo A, Pisano I, Topakas E, Agrimi G.

papers.title: Targeted immune modulation through smart biomaterials and programmable biopharmaceuticals: A review.
papers.abstract: Immune-mediated diseases remain a major global health challenge, while current immunotherapies are often limited by systemic toxicity, poor tissue selectivity, and insufficient control over immune responses. This review examines recent advances in targeted immune modulation through smart biomaterials, programmable biopharmaceuticals, and hybrid biomaterial-biologic systems. A structured literature review was conducted using peer-reviewed studies published between 2022 and 2026 from major biomedical databases. The reviewed evidence indicates that smart biomaterials can respond to disease-associated microenvironmental signals, such as pH changes, hypoxia, oxidative stress, and inflammatory enzymes, enabling localized and context-dependent therapeutic activity. Programmable biopharmaceuticals further enhance precision by directing immune-cell behavior and molecular signaling through engineered biological mechanisms. In addition, hybrid biomaterial-biologic platforms combine environmental responsiveness with the potency of biologic therapeutics, improving immune targeting and reducing unintended systemic effects. Collectively, these technologies support a transition from conventional systemic immunomodulation toward adaptive and site-specific immune control. Despite significant progress, important challenges remain, including biological complexity, manufacturing scalability, long-term safety assessment, and regulatory translation. Nevertheless, the convergence of biomaterials science, synthetic biology, and immunoengineering is creating new opportunities for precision immunotherapy. Targeted immune modulation through programmable and responsive therapeutic systems represents a promising framework for developing safer, more effective, and clinically durable next-generation immunomodulatory therapies.
papers.authors: Yousefi H, Moradian C.

papers.title: AI-Facilitated Discovery of Microbiome-Originated Antimicrobial Peptides: A Perspective on Combating Antibiotic Resistance Within Public Health and Food Safety Frameworks.
papers.abstract: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) demands innovative therapeutic strategies beyond conventional antibiotics. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), particularly those originating from the human, animal, and environmental microbiome, represent a promising frontier within public health microbiology and microbial food safety. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have revolutionized the discovery pipeline, enabling high-throughput mining of metagenomic data and de novo generation of novel peptide sequences. This perspective review synthesizes recent breakthroughs in AI-driven discovery of microbiome-originated AMPs, examines their preclinical efficacy against multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens under One Health and climate-sensitive frameworks and application in infectious disease treatment and discusses translational challenges including pharmacokinetics, toxicity, manufacturing scalability, and applications in food preservation and water safety. We argue that the convergence of microbiome science, deep learning, and synthetic biology positions AI-discovered AMPs as viable next-generation interventions against antibiotic resistance across human, animal, and environmental domains.
papers.authors: Atuahene PY, Stevenson B, Sang Y.

papers.title: CLEAN Database: providing enzyme function coverage for over 55 million sequences.
papers.abstract: Enzyme function annotation is critical for decoding biological systems and enabling rational enzyme design. However, experimentally characterized enzyme functions remain available for only a small fraction of known protein sequences, resulting in a widening gap between rapidly expanding sequence space and reliable functional assignments. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have accelerated enzyme function annotation by facilitating accurate and high-throughput prediction from protein sequences. Here, we present CLEAN Database (CLEAN DB), a comprehensive resource encompassing >55 million enzyme function annotations across 1 098 305 strains, predicted by the CLEAN AI model. The database features an intuitive web interface that enables users to efficiently search, explore, and download enzyme function data through flexible query options. Additionally, powered by a protein language model, CLEAN DB supports mutation effect prediction through interactive heatmaps, structural overlays, and tabular data visualizations. We anticipate that CLEAN DB will serve as a valuable platform for advancing enzyme discovery and applications in synthetic biology, metabolic engineering, enzyme engineering, retrosynthesis, and drug discovery. The database is freely available at https://cleandb.platform.moleculemaker.org/.
papers.authors: Yuan L, Li JC, Wen M, Bianchi DM, Arneson K, Guo B, Lambert S, Stephens C, Yu T, Fu L, Pond C, Berry MJ, Zhao H.

papers.title: Deep Learning and Domain Expertise for Fabricating High-Performance Biosensors.
papers.abstract: Transcription factor-based biosensors are essential for the scalable bioproduction of plant natural products. However, a major bottleneck in developing high-performance biosensors is the engineering of responsive promoters due to the vast sequence space and poorly understood sequence-function relationships. Here, we extend our previously published DeepSEED framework into an artificial intelligence-driven pipeline for efficient and extensible biosensor-responsive promoter optimization. This strategy integrates deep learning with domain-specific biological expertise. By fixing core promoter elements, varying the number and position of transcription factor binding sites (TFBSs) to define promoter backbones, and subsequently optimizing the flanking sequences, we enable the de novo design of promoters. We systematically apply this strategy to optimize a panel of biosensors across different transcription factors and regulatory modes, including four metabolite-responsive biosensors and a quorum-sensing-based environmental sensor. The resulting biosensors exhibit diverse dynamic behaviors with markedly improved sensitivity, expanded dynamic range, and increased maximum output. For instance, the optimized naringenin biosensor demonstrates a 32-fold broader dynamic range and a 27-fold higher maximum output compared to its parent. To illustrate its utility in metabolic engineering, we employed a DeepSEED-designed promoter to dynamically regulate a p-coumaric acid biosynthesis pathway, boosting production by 117.0%. Our work extends the previously published DeepSEED framework into a powerful pipeline for biosensor optimization and delivers a portfolio of high-performance regulatory elements, addressing a critical need and facilitating the development of more intelligent and productive metabolic engineering systems.
papers.authors: Xiao ML, Zhang P, Li Z, Lin NQ, Wang X, Liu JZ.

papers.title: Endophytes for climate-resilient agriculture: Mechanisms and systems-level insights.
papers.abstract: Endophytic bacteria and fungi that asymptomatically colonise plant tissues represent promising biological resources for developing sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural systems. These beneficial microorganisms establish intimate associations with crops and modulate plant growth, nutrient acquisition, immune responses, and stress physiology through diverse biochemical and molecular mechanisms. Endophytes enhance crop performance by producing phytohormones, solubilising and mobilising essential nutrients, improving nutrient-use efficiency, suppressing phytopathogens, inducing systemic resistance, and regulating plant metabolic and antioxidant responses. These functions can improve crop tolerance to major climate-associated stresses, including drought, salinity, heat, and nutrient limitations, while contributing to stable growth and yield under changing environmental conditions. Their potential as biofertilizers, biocontrol agents, biostimulants, and components of integrated crop management offers opportunities to reduce dependence on synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and promote environmentally sustainable agricultural production. This review critically synthesises current knowledge of endophyte diversity, crop colonisation, host specificity, plant-microbe signalling, and mechanisms underlying growth promotion, disease suppression, nutrient acquisition, and abiotic stress tolerance. Particular emphasis is placed on multi-omics and systems-level approaches that reveal endophyte-mediated regulation of plant metabolism, immunity, and microbiome assembly. The review also evaluates major constraints limiting agricultural translation, including inconsistent field performance, environmental adaptability, formulation and delivery, host microbe compatibility, ecological interactions, biosafety, and regulatory requirements. Finally, integration of multi-omics, microbiome engineering, synthetic biology, and precision agriculture is proposed as a pathway for developing robust endophyte-based technologies and microbial consortia. Such approaches could facilitate the transition toward low-input, resource-efficient, productive, and climate-resilient agriculture while strengthening long-term food security.
papers.authors: Singh N, Mohanta YK, Priyadarshi N, Das D, Sharifi-Rad M.

papers.title: Enzymatic PET depolymerization: a review of engineering biocatalysts and systems for efficient plastic deconstruction.
papers.abstract: The ever-increasing accumulation of polyethylene terephthalate (PET) waste poses a severe threat to global ecosystems and human health. Biological upcycling (integrating enzymatic depolymerization with microbial conversion of the resulting monomers) has emerged as a promising approach to overcome the limitations of traditional mechanical and chemical recycling. This review provides a systematic and critical synthesis of recent advances in PET bio-upcycling, covering the period from 2016 to 2026. We first discuss the discovery, classification, structural features, and catalytic mechanisms of PET-hydrolyzing enzymes, highlighting the rate-limiting constraints imposed by glass transition temperature, substrate crystallinity, interfacial interactions, and product inhibition. We then evaluate protein engineering strategies that have dramatically enhanced thermostability, substrate binding, and multi-enzyme synergy, yielding benchmark variants capable of near-complete depolymerization of post-consumer PET within hours to days. Concurrent innovations in whole-cell biocatalysis, enzyme immobilization, surface display, and microbial consortia are examined, with emphasis on how metabolic division of labor and substrate channeling can alleviate product inhibition and process mixed plastic waste. We also summarize metabolic engineering efforts that have enabled conversion of PET-derived terephthalic acid (TPA) and ethylene glycol (EG) into more than 25 value-added products, including biopolymers, platform chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and specialty compounds. Finally, we discuss remaining technological barriers, economic feasibility, and future frontiers (including computational enzyme design, synthetic consortia, tandem chemo-biological processes, and industrial-scale demonstration) and propose a phased roadmap for industrial translation. This review aims to provide a comprehensive resource for advancing PET bio-upcycling from laboratory innovation toward practical implementation in a circular plastics economy.
papers.authors: Liu F, Wang T, Li N, Liu XH, Xu N, Zhu F.

papers.title: From gut microbiome to aging brain: Butyrate as a neurogeroscience effector.
papers.abstract: Aging-related cognitive decline is increasingly linked to disruption of the microbiome-gut-brain axis, in which age-associated dysbiosis progressively reduces butyrate production, a short-chain fatty acid and central neuroactive metabolite generated by bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber. Experimental studies indicate that butyrate can influence multiple processes relevant to brain aging, including histone deacetylase activity, neuroinflammatory signaling, microglial phenotypes, blood-brain barrier integrity, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis. Through these mechanisms, butyrate may modulate several molecular and cellular processes involved in brain aging, although evidence for direct causal effects in the human brain remains limited. Preclinical studies report neuroprotective effects across several models of aging and neurological disease; however, direct evidence in humans remains limited and largely associative or indirect. Therefore, this review critically synthesizes current evidence on microbiome-derived butyrate in brain aging, encompassing its microbial production and age-related alterations, molecular and cellular mechanisms, associations with neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric conditions, and emerging strategies for therapeutic modulation and delivery. It examines emerging biotechnological strategies - including prodrug design, nanoparticle- and liposomal-based delivery systems, gut-targeted formulations, and microbiome engineering - all developed to overcome the blood-brain barrier and restore therapeutically relevant butyrate concentrations in the aging brain. By bridging fundamental microbiome biology and translational neuroscience, this review positions butyrate as a mechanistically grounded neurogeroscience effector and charts a roadmap for its application in promoting brain health across the aging continuum.
papers.authors: Mitrea L, Calinoiu LF, Martau GA, Teleky BE, Cocean AM, Odocheanu R, Stefanescu BE, Vodnar DC.

papers.title: Host-Shaped Microbial Metabolite Signaling in the AKI-to-CKDTransition: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Boundaries.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) increases the subsequent risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the transition is shaped by the quality of tubular repair rather than nephron loss alone. We frame the gut-kidney axis as a bidirectional host-microbial system in which AKI-related inflammation, impaired solute clearance, altered tubular transport, intestinal barrier dysfunction, medications, diet, and intestinal transit may redirect microbial metabolic output during recovery. Repair-disrupting candidates, including trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), indoxyl sulfate (IS), p-cresyl sulfate (PCS), and broader aromatic solute burden, are evaluated alongside repair-permissive candidates such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), selected indoles, and bile acids; polyamines are treated as bidirectional and stage-dependent. We connect these exposures to mitochondrial recovery, cell-cycle arrest, senescence, immune recruitment, endothelial stress, and fibroblast activation, while distinguishing microbial production from host transformation, renal clearance, and tubular uptake. Direct human AKI-to-CKD evidence remains limited, and antibiotic-depletion studies cannot isolate a single metabolite pathway. Translational studies should therefore combine longitudinal blood, urine, and fecal profiling with AKI etiology, treatment exposures, tubular injury markers, spatial kidney biology, and target-engagement endpoints.
papers.authors: Xu Z, Chen W, Lu F.

papers.title: Host-Specific Metabolic Engineering for Microbial Production of Fucosyllactoses.
papers.abstract: Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are a diverse group of bioactive glycans that play important roles in infant health by modulating the gut microbiota, inhibiting pathogen adhesion, and promoting immune development. Among them, 2'-fucosyllactose (2'-FL) and 3-fucosyllactose (3-FL) have attracted considerable attention owing to their established health benefits and increasing applications in infant formula and functional foods. Microbial biosynthesis has emerged as a sustainable and scalable alternative to chemical synthesis and enzymatic production. This review summarizes recent advances in microbial FL production using Escherichia coli, Saccharomyces cerevisiae , and Yarrowia lipolytica , with emphasis on host-specific metabolic engineering strategies. Key engineering approaches, including GDP-L-fucose biosynthesis, lactose uptake, fucosyltransferase (FT) optimization, transporter engineering, and fermentation process development, are systematically discussed and compared across microbial hosts. The review highlights the distinct advantages and limitations of bacterial and yeast platforms, including product secretion, intracellular FL accumulation, carbon flux distribution, and redox balance. Finally, current bottlenecks and future engineering opportunities are discussed, including transporter optimization, host-specific metabolic regulation, and industrial process development. These advances provide valuable insights into the development of efficient, safe, and economically viable microbial cell factories for the sustainable production of FL and other fucosylated HMOs.
papers.authors: Kim BM, Jang YJ, Song HY, Jung SC, Shin J, Lee JW.

papers.title: Late-Stage Large Extracellular Vesicles Reprogram CHO Cell Metabolism in a Glutamine-Dependent Mode and Promote Antibody-Productivity to Cell-Growth Tradeoff.
papers.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are mediators of intercellular communication, yet their impact on Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cell physiology and bioprocess performance remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated whether small EVs (sEVs) and large EVs (LgEVs) that accumulate during fed-batch and perfusion cultures modulate CHO cell growth, metabolism, apoptosis, and monoclonal antibody (mAb) production. EVs isolated from early- and late-stage cultures were added to fresh CHO cultures grown with or without glutamine supplementation. Only LgEVs had a significant impact. Late-stage LgEVs markedly altered CHO-cell behavior, reducing cell proliferation, increasing apoptosis under glutamine-limited conditions, and substantially enhancing mAb productivity in a dose-dependent manner. Glutamine supplementation largely alleviated the growth-inhibitory and pro-apoptotic effects of LgEVs while preserving their positive impact on productivity, suggesting that glutamine mitigated the EV-mediated stress without affecting the productivity enhancement. Metabolic analyses revealed increased glucose consumption, a glutamine-dependent shift between glycine and alanine overflow metabolism, and remodeling of amino-acid utilization. Metabolic flux analysis further demonstrated enhanced glycolytic overflow and increased reliance on amino acid-supported anaplerosis. Conversely, selective removal of LgEVs from perfusion medium significantly improved cell expansion without reducing antibody production, supporting an inhibitory role for late-stage LgEVs. These LgEVs were enriched in let-7 family miRNAs and miR-21, consistent with RNAseq analyses demonstrating stress-associated enrichment of these miRNAs in CHO EVs and with functional studies showing that let-7a and miR-21reduce CHO-cell growth. Together, these observations suggest that selective miRNA loading contributes to the growth, metabolic, and productivity phenotypes elicited by late-stage LgEVs. Our findings identify LgEVs in CHO-K1 can act as endogenous regulators of CHO-cell physiology thus deserving attention for optimizing high-density fed-batch and perfusion biomanufacturing processes.

papers.title: Metabolic Competition-Driven Antitumor Immunity of glpX -Deficient Engineered Salmonella via Glucose Deprivation and STING Activation in Bladder Cancer.
papers.abstract: Background: Bacteria-mediated cancer therapy is emerging as a promising approach due to its low cost, scalability, and sustained efficacy. While bacterial immunomodulation has been extensively studied, the role of bacterial metabolic competition, particularly for glucose, in tumor suppression remains unclear. We aimed to investigate how engineered Salmonella strains exploit metabolic competition to trigger antitumor immunity and improve therapeutic outcomes in bladder cancer models. Methods: Using genetic screening, we generated a gluconeogenesis-deficient Salmonella strain, the AISIH strain with the glpX gene knocked out (GLA1), with enhanced glucose uptake. In vitro and in vivo assays were performed to assess tumor cell glucose deprivation, mitochondrial stress, cytosolic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, and activation of the cGAS/STING pathway. An engineered strain, GLA2, was generated from the AISIH strain by knockout of the glpX gene and was subsequently further engineered to locally deliver an anti-tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) nanobody under quorum-sensing control. Efficacy was evaluated in subcutaneous and orthotopic bladder cancer models, with analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, dendritic cell (DC) maturation, and T cell priming. Results: GLA1 competitively depleted glucose in the bladder tumor microenvironment, inducing energy stress, mitochondrial damage, and mtDNA release, which noncanonically activated the STING pathway. This promoted type I interferon production, DC maturation, and antitumor immune responses. However, TNF-α-mediated vascular abnormalities limited efficacy. GLA2 normalized tumor vasculature via local anti-TNF-α delivery, enhancing nutrient competition and immune activation. Both strains markedly suppressed tumor growth, with GLA2 showing superior efficacy due to synergistic metabolic and immune reprogramming. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that bacterial competition for glucose is a pivotal mechanism of antitumor activity in bladder cancer, linking metabolic stress to STING-dependent immune activation. Engineered Salmonella strains that combine enhanced glucose uptake with local vascular normalization offer a robust platform for bladder cancer. These findings highlight a novel strategy to integrate microbial metabolic engineering with immune modulation, providing a foundation for precision bacteriotherapy in oncology.
